summary: Anant Shankhdhar from Risa Labs presents their system for automating oncology prior authorization workflows end-to-end. The workflow involves intaking daily orders, verifying patient eligibility (eligibility and benefits verification), determining which drugs require authorization (categorized as NAR/no auth required, auth on file, or auth required), and submitting to payers. The goal was to run certain orders directly to submission without human touch, requiring confident identification of which orders can proceed without verification. The system uses four agents working as a DAG. The EV agent performs eligibility and benefits verification through a unified service connecting to different payer sources via APIs or RPA (browser automation), outputting normalized coverage results processed by a deterministic decision engine. To scale RPA integrations, they built a repository of custom actions, LLM-based config generation for new portals, and a self-healing loop to handle runtime failures. The auth agent determines drug authorization status. A simple LLM extraction pipeline from patient notes had issues with insufficient data and non-determinism. To increase confidence, they added evidence sources: authorization letters from previous patient runs and a payer rule knowledge base (SQL database built from portal checks and LLM extractions) for NAR cases. They reconcile evidence from multiple sources, only extracting auth statuses with higher confidence, enabling no-touch processing for certain orders. The medical necessity agent handles auth-required drugs by reading patient notes and policy criteria, querying a patient medical graph (biomarkers extracted per patient), and using an LLM to answer clinical questions with supportive and contradictory facts. A confidence score determines whether cases proceed automatically or escalate to clinicians. The submission agent uses customized per-payer integrations with LLM-driven config and a tools repository to submit information back to payers. In conclusion, the no-touch share is growing across every order type. The team started with deterministic checks, deployed agents where rules could not decide, used multi-source evidence to increase confidence over single sources, added self-healing to scale RPA, and added a reasoning layer for cases requiring authentic authorization. The agents, initially built for oncology prior authorization, are now being extended to more general workflows where the medical necessity agent can answer questions specific to any patient workflow.

sections.title: Introduction and Workflow Overview
sections.summary: Anant Shankhdhar introduces Risa's work automating oncology prior authorization workflows. The workflow involves intaking orders, verifying patient eligibility, and categorizing drugs into NAR (no auth required), auth on file, or auth required pathways. Currently human review is required before submission; the goal is to eliminate human touch for eligible orders.

sections.title: Problem Statement and Agent Architecture
sections.summary: The task is to confidently identify orders that can proceed to submission without human verification. Four agents were built: EV agent (eligibility and benefits verification), auth agent (drug authorization status), necessity agent (clinical reasoning), and submission agent.

sections.title: EV Agent: Unified Service and RPA
sections.summary: Insurance data is scattered across portals, APIs, and documents. A unified service connects to payer sources via API or RPA, outputting normalized coverage results. A coverage orchestrator routes to API or RPA path, and a deterministic engine checks coverage status. To scale RPA, they built a repository of custom actions, LLM-based config generation for new portals, and a self-healing loop for runtime failures.

sections.title: Auth Agent: Drug Authorization Status
sections.summary: An LLM extraction pipeline categorizes drugs from patient notes into NAR, auth on file, or auth required. Issues arose: notes lacked sufficient data and LLM extraction is non-deterministic, meaning outputs cannot be blindly trusted and still require human review.

sections.title: Evidence Reconciliation for Higher Confidence
sections.summary: To address non-determinism, two additional evidence sources were added: authorization letters from previous patient runs (for auth on file cases) and a payer rule knowledge base (SQL database from portal checks and LLM extractions for NAR cases). Evidence is reconciled across sources, and auth statuses are only extracted with higher confidence. This enabled complete elimination of certain orders from human review.

sections.title: Payer Rule Knowledge Base Construction
sections.summary: The payer rule knowledge base was built from time-based documents using configurable LLM extraction, yielding drug-wise constraints per payer. Historical organization-level treatment patterns and regular portal checks supplement this data. Combined with deterministic checks, this moved the needle forward by enabling no-touch on a certain set of orders.

sections.title: Medical Necessity Agent
sections.summary: For auth-required drugs, clinical reasoning is needed. The medical necessity agent reads patient notes and policy criteria, queries a patient medical graph (biomarkers extracted per patient), and uses an LLM to generate answered questionnaires with supportive and contradictory facts. A confidence score determines whether cases proceed automatically or escalate to clinicians. A publication is referenced.

sections.title: Submission Agent and Full Pipeline
sections.summary: The submission agent assembles all information and submits back to payers. Similar to the EV agent, it uses customized per-payer integrations built with LLM-driven config and a tools repository. The full pipeline graph is presented as the culmination of the entire journey from data fetching through eligibility, authorization status extraction, medical necessity validation, and submission.

sections.title: Conclusion: Growing No-Touch and Generalization
sections.summary: The green parts of the pipeline diagram show cases going without human touch: when eligibility verification passes and enough information is found to proceed through medical necessity evaluation and submission. The agents, initially built for oncology prior authorization, are now being extended to more general workflows where the medical necessity agent can answer questions specific to any patient workflow. In conclusion, the no-touch share is growing across every order type through layered improvements: deterministic checks first, agents where rules cannot decide, multi-source evidence to beat single-source confidence, self-healing to scale RPA, and a reasoning layer for cases requiring authentic authorization.

demonstrations: Unified service connecting to multiple payer sources with normalized output
LLM-based config generation for building RPA integrations for new portals
Self-healing loop that identifies and mitigates RPA failures during production hours
Multi-source evidence reconciliation pipeline combining patient notes, authorization letters, and payer rule knowledge base
Payer rule knowledge base (SQL) construction from portal checks, LLM extractions, and historical data
Patient medical graph queried for biomarkers to answer clinical questions
LLM answering clinical questions with supportive and contradictory facts plus confidence scoring
Full pipeline graph showing green no-touch cases from eligibility through medical necessity to submission
limitations: LLM extraction is non-deterministic and cannot be blindly trusted without human review
Patient notes often lack sufficient data for reliable extraction
RPA automations are fragile and may break during runtime
Custom integrations for different portals are not scalable without LLM-assisted config generation
Some cases still require human clinician escalation when confidence is insufficient
Multi-source evidence reconciliation only enables no-touch for certain order types, not all
quantitativeClaims: Supporting care for more than 100,000 patients
Agents combined do the work of hundreds of medical workers per day
100+ browsers running in parallel on Kubernetes for submissions
System handles thousands of submissions per hour at full capacity
